framework.name: Illinois Learning Standards for Social Science (Economics and Financial Literacy, 9–12), with the Council for Economic Education Voluntary National Content Standards in Economics
framework.note: Codes are Illinois 9–12 economics and financial-literacy standards (SS.EC.x.9-12, SS.EC.FL.x.9-12) and CEE Voluntary National Content Standards in Economics, 2nd ed. 2010 (CEE 1–20); alignment was made by the course author and is not a certification by either body.

standards.text: Analyze how incentives drive choices that can yield policies whose costs and benefits fall unevenly on different groups
Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to build an argument for or against a solution to an economic issue
Productive resources are limited, so people cannot have everything and must choose some things and give up others
Good decisions compare the additional costs and benefits of alternatives, since most choices are a little more or less
Goods and services can be allocated by different methods, and people must choose which methods to use
Weigh the costs and benefits of different strategies, such as education and career choices, for increasing income
Analyze how incentives shape what a market system produces and how goods are distributed
People usually respond predictably to positive and negative incentives
Markets form where buyers and sellers interact, setting prices that allocate scarce goods and services
Prices signal and give incentives to buyers and sellers; when supply or demand shifts, prices adjust
Use costs and benefits to evaluate how well government policies improve market outcomes
Prices send signals and incentives to buyers and sellers, so blocking price adjustment distorts those incentives
Government has an economic role where a policy's benefits exceed its costs, such as public goods and externalities
Government policies sometimes cost more than they deliver, owing to voter, official and special-interest incentives
Institutions, including clearly defined and enforced property rights, are essential to a market economy
Analyze how incentives shape what a market system produces and how goods are distributed
Competition among sellers usually lowers costs and prices and pushes producers to make what consumers want
Entrepreneurs take risks to organize resources and bring new products and production methods to market
Institutions such as corporations, banks, labor unions and legal systems help people and groups reach their goals
Most people's income depends on the market value of the productive resources, including labor, they sell
Investment in capital, technology and people's health, education and training drives growth and future living standards
Unemployment and inflation both impose costs; unemployment rises in recessions and falls in recoveries
The money supply affects the overall price level, and inflation is a rising price level that erodes money's value
Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to build an argument for or against a solution to an economic issue
Fluctuations in national income, employment and prices arise from the spending and production decisions of all sectors
Federal budget policy and Federal Reserve monetary policy influence overall employment, output and prices
Government policies sometimes cost more than they deliver, owing to political incentives and special interests
Money makes it easier to trade, borrow, save, invest and compare values, and its quantity affects prices
Inflation-adjusted interest rates rise and fall to balance saving with borrowing, allocating resources across time
Federal Reserve monetary policy and federal budget policy influence overall employment, output and prices
Weigh the costs and benefits of different forms of credit and the effect of interest
Compare saving and investment options by expected return and risk
Use costs and benefits to evaluate how well government policies improve market outcomes
Analyze how incentives drive choices that can yield policies whose costs and benefits fall unevenly on different groups
Voluntary exchange happens only when all parties expect to gain, whether within a nation or across borders
When people, regions and nations specialize in lowest-cost production and trade, production and consumption rise
Government has an economic role where benefits exceed costs, and its taxes and policies affect people's incomes
